ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses 2.20–21
note: Gregory reads the unconsumed burning bush as a figure of the virgin conception: divine fire is present without consuming. This Christian interpretation expands the commentary's sacred, non-hell fire beyond navigation and judgment.

Justin identifies the one who appeared and spoke to Moses in the bush's flame with the pre-existent Christ. This Christian reading changes the identity of the voice at the fire while preserving the fire-theophany shared with the commentary.

basis: flaming fire for those who reject the message
note: The commentary says the wretched turns away from admonition and enters the great fire; Paul describes judgment in flaming fire against those who do not know God or obey the gospel, making the rejection-to-fire sequence explicit.

The Lord is revealed in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel. This joins rejection of a divine message to fiery judgment, as the commentary joins turning from reminder to the great fire.

Tongues as of fire appear, divide, and rest on each person at Pentecost. This non-punitive communal fire offers a Christian counterpart to the commentary's blessed fire around which divine speech and glorification occur.

On Malta the islanders kindle a fire and welcome the shipwrecked group because of cold and rain. Its human fire supplies warmth and shelter, the non-punitive use the commentary sets beside entry into the great fire.

The commentary invokes Moses seeing fire before hearing a call; Stephen recounts the angel appearing in a flame from a bush and introduces Moses' commission, preserving the scene in an early Christian retelling.

basis: flame of fire in a bush
note: Stephen retells that an angel appeared to Moses in wilderness Sinai in a flame of fire in a bush; it is the New Testament's direct recollection of the fire scene.
Moses sees the sight, approaches to inspect it, and then the Lord's voice comes. The sequence matches the commentary's visible fire leading to a divine address.

The speaking Lord announces that he has seen Israel's affliction and sends Moses to Egypt. This Christian retelling preserves the commissioned response to the fire-theophany that the commentary calls divine choosing.

The commentary presents the great fire as the wretched person's punishment; Hebrews recalls faithful people who quenched the power of fire, giving a Christian counter-example in which fidelity protects from its force.
Hebrews recalls Sinai as a mountain with blazing fire, gloom, and tempest. It receives the Moses/Sinai fire tradition that frames the commentary's Mount Ṭūr address.

Because believers receive an unshakable kingdom, they are urged to offer God acceptable worship with reverence and awe. It places worship as response within Hebrews' immediately fire-marked Sinai discourse.
The commentary moves from fire at Moses' call to worship and prayer; Hebrews calls God a consuming fire in a passage urging reverent worship, holding judgment-fire and devotion together.

Hebrews calls God a consuming fire. Together with its preceding exhortation to worship, it provides a Christian configuration in which reverent worship and divine fire belong together, not only as opposites.

Jesus calls himself the light of the world and says a follower will not walk in darkness. Though not a fire scene, it is a precise Christian counterpart to the commentary's fire seen from afar as a guide toward the way.
Sodom and Gomorrah undergo a penalty of eternal fire and stand as an example. It joins the commentary's two functions of fire: judgment made into a warning or reminder for readers.

The commentary says the condemned neither die nor live and endure the fire's severity; Luke depicts a dead rich man conscious in flame and asking for relief, adding a specific afterlife image of felt torment.

basis: agony and heat in the flame
note: The rich man in Hades asks for water to cool his tongue because he is in agony in the flame. It supplies the specific embodied heat and suffering that the commentary draws from the Arabic sense of entering and bearing fire.

The commentary connects non-ending punishment with fire that does not spare; Jesus applies Isaiah's undying-worm and unquenched-fire language to Gehenna, making the prophetic image an explicit warning about final judgment.
Jesus's Gehenna saying retains the undying worm and unquenched fire. It supplies a concrete Christian form of the commentary's fire that neither releases nor spares its victim.
The commentary identifies the wretched one as entering the great fire; the judgment scene assigns the condemned to eternal fire, sharpening the relation between moral fate and fire.
In the judgment scene, those at the left are told to depart into fire prepared for the devil and angels. It is a direct Christian counterpart to the wretched person entering the great fire.
The commentary pairs remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer; Jesus' prayer begins by asking that the Father's name be hallowed, a concrete prayer-formula parallel while the verbs differ.

basis: fire and sulfur for the worshiper
note: That worshiper is tormented with fire and sulfur before holy angels and the Lamb. This explicitly makes corrupt worship, rather than prayer to God, lead to punitive fire.

The commentary's damned neither die nor live and the Saqar fire does not relent; Revelation says the smoke of the beast-worshippers' torment rises forever and they have no rest, an analogous account of unending punishment with a distinct image.
The smoke of that torment rises forever and its worshipers have no rest day or night. It adds an enduring experiential dimension to the commentary's account of entering and bearing the great fire.

John names worship of the beast and receipt of its mark as the opposed cultic act. It supplies a concrete alternative to the commentary's person who remembers the Lord's name and prays; its fire consequence is named in the next verse.

Those victorious over the beast stand at the sea of glass mingled with fire, holding God's harps. It reverses the commentary's fire-bound wretch by placing victorious worshipers beside fire rather than as its sufferers.

basis: song of Moses at the fire scene
note: The victors sing the song of Moses and the Lamb, praising God's great and marvelous works. This adds Moses and praise to the preceding fire-mingled scene, echoing the commentary's Moses-fire journey toward worship.

The song asks who will not fear the Lord, glorify his Name, and worship him. Its Name-and-worship formula completes the fire-and-Moses sequence with a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's remembering the Lord's Name and praying.

ref: Song of the Three Young Men 3:52-56
note: The commentary places glorification at Moses' fire and contrasts prayer with damnation; the youths' song blesses and praises God amid the furnace, adding a liturgical voice from inside a fire.

basis: ordinary fire as a foretaste of Gehenna
note: The rabbinic maxim calls ordinary fire one-sixtieth of Gehenna. It supplies a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the commentary's claim that a small human fire is a reminder of the great punitive fire.

The commentary makes Moses' fire a route to divine address; the midrash reads the thornbush's burning without destruction as God's presence with Israel in affliction, turning the fire into a sign of solidarity and survival.

Exodus Rabbah reads the burning, unconsumed thornbush as God's presence with Israel in affliction. That reading makes the Sinai fire a sign of solidarity rather than merely route, fuel, or punishment.

Judith's judgment hymn says that God sends fire and worms into the flesh of hostile nations, with pain without end. Its bodily punitive fire is a close Jewish parallel to the commentary's skin-burning account of the great fire.

Azariah stands in the furnace and begins a spoken prayer blessing the God of the ancestors. The Greek-Jewish addition counterposes prayer inside a human furnace to the commentary's division of the prayerful person from the fire-bound one.

David builds an altar, offers sacrifice, calls to YHWH, and receives an answer in fire from heaven. It provides another single-verse scene in which worshipful invocation, rather than entry into punishment, is answered by fire.

basis: call the Name; answer by fire
note: Elijah frames the Carmel test as calling on a god's name, with the god who answers by fire shown to be God. It gives a concrete biblical conjunction of divine Name, prayer, and fire beside the commentary's remembrance of the Name and prayer at Moses's fire.

basis: Elijah's prayer names God before fire
note: The commentary pairs remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer; Elijah invokes the God of the ancestors and asks that Israel know YHWH is God before fire answers, joining prayer, divine identity, and fire.

basis: fire descends in answer to prayer
note: The commentary contrasts going toward a guiding fire with entering a punitive one; after Elijah's prayer, fire falls from YHWH and consumes the offering, reversing the human direction toward fire into a divine response.
The commentary's Moses scene ends in worship and prayer at a fire; after the fire on Carmel, the people fall on their faces and confess YHWH as God, giving a distinct fire-to-worship sequence.

The commentary's Moses hears the divine address at a fire; at Horeb Elijah sees wind, earthquake, and fire, but this verse says YHWH is not in the fire and is encountered in the quiet sound, a distinct counter-scene about revelation.

basis: fire followed by thin quiet sound
note: At Horeb the sequence is earthquake, fire, then qôl demamah daqqah, a thin quiet sound. That order contrasts with the commentary's Moses, whose call is located at the fire.

The three Judeans say the God they serve can rescue them from the blazing furnace. This reverses the commentary's fire/prayer polarity: service of God is voiced at the edge of fire as confidence of rescue.
The commentary stresses the great fire's heat and severity; Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace heated seven times more than usual, intensifying the furnace image beyond an ordinary flame.

basis: fire kills those who cast the men in
note: The commentary describes the damned as enduring the fire's heat; Daniel says the furnace's flame kills the men who throw the faithful into it, while the next scene preserves those inside, distinguishing the fire's effects.

The commentary presents entry into the great fire as punishment for the wretched; Daniel sees the three faithful men walking unharmed inside the furnace with a fourth figure, reversing the expected result of fire-entry.

The Qur'anic Moses scene has blessing and glorification spoken at the fire; after the furnace rescue, Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of the three men, connecting fire, deliverance, and praise in a different scene.

The commentary explicitly reports Arabic nūr and nār together through illumination, while biblical Aramaic uses nūrā for the furnace fire; this supplies a concrete fire-word cognate without proving the commentary's etymology.

Biblical Aramaic calls the blazing furnace נוּר. Its nūr “fire” is a controlled Semitic beside-word for the commentary's Arabic النار/nūr discussion, while the furnace context prevents importing its road-light sense.

The commentary distinguishes the fire verb ṣ-l-y from the prayer verb ṣ-l-w; Daniel's Aramaic verb for his three daily prayers is from the prayer sense, a close Semitic cognate that supports the prayer-side echo without merging the Qur'anic roots.

The commentary contrasts the one who prays with those who say they were not among the prayerful; Daniel keeps praying and thanking God three times daily despite the royal decree, giving a concrete scene of persevering prayer.

Daniel kneels toward Jerusalem, prays, and gives thanks; the Aramaic verb צְלָא is the prayer-side cognate beside the commentary's فَصَلَّى. It reinforces the stated sound-echo with fire vocabulary without collapsing Arabic ص ل و and ص ل ي.

basis: voice from the midst of fire
note: Moses tells Israel that YHWH spoke from the midst of fire while they saw no form, only a voice. It sharpens the commentary's voiced fire while keeping the speaker distinct from the visible flame.

Moses says God showed Israel his great fire on earth and they heard words from the midst of fire. Its explicit great-fire/voice pairing reframes the commentary's opposition of the greatest fire and Moses's greatest signs.

The commentary includes roasting meat under Arabic ṣ-l-y; Exodus names the Passover lamb as roasted with fire, a plausible weak-consonant Semitic cognate for that cooking sense, not for the distinct prayer root.

The commentary records roasting meat under Arabic ṣ-l-y; Exodus uses the Hebrew roasting form for the Passover lamb, a possible cognate for that culinary sense, though the weak final consonants make the relationship uncertain.

Passover flesh must be eaten roasted with fire (צְלִי־אֵשׁ). Hebrew צלי/צלה is a likely cognate of the commentary's Arabic ص ل ي cooking sense, giving a concrete domestic-ritual use beside its suffering-in-fire sense.

The commentary recalls fires lit as waymarks so people could find and follow a route; Exodus says YHWH led Israel by a pillar of fire at night, an explicit divine fire that lights and guides a journey.
The pillar of fire gives Israel light so they can travel by night; it is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's distant fire lit as a route-marker and to its huda/guidance link.

basis: pillar of fire turns on Egypt
note: During the night, YHWH looks down on Egypt's army through the pillar of fire and cloud and throws it into panic. This gives the commentary's route-guiding fire a second biblical role: the same wilderness fire also separates and judges those opposing God's deliverance.

Sinai smokes because YHWH descends upon it in fire, and the mountain trembles. Its mountain-scale fire is a close Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's fire seen at the side of al-Ṭūr, distinct from the contained bush.
The commentary locates Moses' sighting at the side of Tur; Exodus first brings Moses' flock to Horeb, the mountain of God, grounding the shared fire encounter in its mountain setting.
Exodus places shepherd Moses at Horeb, the mountain of God; it anchors the commentary's Moses seeing fire from the side of al-Ṭūr in the same mountain-call setting.
At the bush God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring Israel out. This makes Exodus's commissioning the counterpart to “I have chosen you; listen to revelation” in the commentary.

The commentary quotes the Qur'anic command at the fire to worship and establish prayer; Exodus says Israel will serve God on this mountain after the bush call, linking the encounter to worship while leaving prayer-for-remembrance distinctive to the Qur'anic wording.
God says Israel will serve God on this mountain after liberation. The mountain fire-call is thus ordered toward worship, as the commentary joins Moses's fire journey to remembrance and prayer.

The commentary's pious person remembers the Lord's name before prayer; at Moses' fire encounter God gives the self-designation “I am who I am,” adding the name's own explanation to the memorial naming in 3:15.

The commentary's pious person remembers the Lord's name and prays; at the bush God gives the name by which generations will remember him, making divine name and remembrance part of the same Mosaic scene.
God gives Moses the enduring Name and calls it his memorial through generations; this places name-remembrance within the same bush commission that the commentary ends in prayer.

The commentary's وَذَكَرَ / dhikr is matched by Hebrew זִכְרִי, “my memorial,” for the Name. The regular Semitic d/z correspondence supports a word-level link without identifying the Arabic roots for prayer and burning.
The commentary has Moses spot a fire and go toward it before the divine address; Exodus places the angel of YHWH in a flame within a bush, making the fire the setting of a call.
An angel appears to Moses in a flame from within a bush that burns without being consumed. It is the closest Hebrew-Bible fire-theophany to the commentary's fire at which Moses is addressed.

basis: great sight, not a practical beacon
note: Moses turns aside to investigate the great sight of a bush that does not burn up; the commentary's Moses first treats the distant fire as a possible ember, warmth, or guide. The different reason for approach is itself illuminating.
The commentary says Moses reaches the fire and is addressed; at the bush God calls “Moses, Moses” and Moses answers, giving the same encounter its direct biblical scene.
After Moses turns aside, God calls “Moses, Moses” from the bush. This supplies the same sequence of approaching visible fire and then receiving divine speech.
The commentary links the fire scene with blessing and glorification; Exodus names the ground around the bush holy and commands Moses to approach reverently, locating sanctity at the fire.
God stops Moses from coming nearer and names the place holy ground; it gives a biblical counterpart for the commentary's blessing and glorification around the fire.

At the end of the bush commission, Moses is told to take the staff with which he will perform signs. It gives the Exodus continuation for the commentary's shift from the greatest fire of judgment to the greatest signs shown to Moses.

basis: a sign shown in Moses' call
note: The commentary cites God's promise to show Moses the greatest signs at the fire; in the continuing bush-call episode Moses' staff becomes a serpent as a sign, giving a concrete counterpart to the signs promised in Qur'an 20:23.
The commentary calls the punishment fire “the great” one; Isaiah describes Topheth's pyre as deep and broad with abundant fire, supplying a concrete biblical scale image for punitive fire.

The commentary identifies the wretched person as entering the great fire; Isaiah asks who can dwell with consuming fire and everlasting burnings, then answers with the righteous, shifting the question from doomed entry to who can endure God's presence.

basis: righteousness as the answer to fire
note: The commentary contrasts one person entering fire with another remembering God and praying; Isaiah's next verse answers who can dwell by naming the one who acts righteously, offering a specific ethical counterpart to the doomed entrant.

When Israel walks through fire, God promises that the flame will not consume it. This covenantal counter-scene reverses the commentary's entry into fire as endurance of its heat while leaving room for its sacred Moses-fire.

The commentary distinguishes ordinary fire used for warmth from the great punitive fire; Isaiah describes a person using part of his wood fire to warm himself and bake bread, then turns to the religious meaning of the remainder.
The commentary cites roasting meat as one sense of ṣ-l-y; Isaiah's man uses the same fire to roast meat and eat, grounding that sense in an ordinary domestic scene.

The commentary calls the kindled small fire a reminder and contrasts it with turning away from admonition; Isaiah makes the remainder of the cooking fire into an idol that the man bows to, a pointed reversal of fire's proper reminder.

basis: self-kindled fire as light, then torment
note: The commentary recalls fire used to find a path and contrasts useful fire with the great punishment; Isaiah addresses people who kindle a fire, walk by its light, and end by lying down in torment.

Those who kindle their own fire and walk by its flame are told that they will lie down in pain. It reverses the commentary's small human fire as useful provision and its warning that an ignored reminder ends in greater fire.

The commentary connects Saqar's “does not leave or spare” with the warning that the damned neither die nor live; Isaiah's final image is corpses of rebels with a worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched.

At the end of Isaiah, those who rebelled against God are an abhorrence, with a fire that is not quenched. It closely matches the commentary's punitive, inescapable great fire rather than a warming or guiding flame.
The commentary glosses al-kubrā through Arabic k-b-r as greatness; Job calls God kabîr, “mighty,” a possible same-root cognate that applies the scale-word to God rather than to a punitive fire.

Nadab and Abihu place fire and incense before YHWH that he had not commanded. The episode requires a distinction between sacred encounter and humanly initiated ritual fire, sharpening the commentary's several ways of approaching fire.

Fire goes out from before YHWH and consumes Nadab and Abihu. Alongside their unauthorized fire in the preceding verse, it complicates the commentary's blessed fire by making uncommanded cultic approach a site of lethal judgment.

The commentary contrasts the wretched who enter the great fire with the pious kept from it; in Hebrew-numbered Malachi, the coming day burns the arrogant and evildoers like an oven, leaving no root or branch.

basis: he name-fearing spared from the burning day
note: The commentary pairs remembering the Lord's name and prayer with safety from fire; the next Hebrew-numbered verse promises healing to those who fear God's name, setting their fate against the wicked burned in 3:19.

basis: fire recalled in communal prayer as guidance
note: The commentary joins fire as a way-sign to remembrance and prayer; Nehemiah's communal confession addresses God while recalling the pillar of fire that lit Israel's path, bringing the same guidance image into a liturgical act.
The commentary treats entry into fire as punishment; after Israel's complaint, YHWH's fire burns at the edge of the camp, giving a concrete wilderness scene of punitive fire.
The commentary contrasts the condemned entrant with the one who remembers God and prays; Moses cries to YHWH and the fire subsides, making prayer an intervention that ends a punitive fire.

The commandment is called a lamp, Torah a light, and corrective reproofs the way of life. Its joined guidance and admonition supplies a Hebrew formulation for the commentary's road-marker fire, huda, and reminder.
The commentary's person remembers the Lord's name and then prays; the psalm summons the worshipper to bless YHWH and not forget his benefits, joining remembrance to liturgical praise.

The commentary develops a fire as a road-marker and links it to being guided; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and light for the path, pairing illumination with guidance without requiring a shared fire scene.

The verse calls God's word a נֵר, “lamp,” for the feet and light for the path. Hebrew nēr is a probable cognate of the commentary's nūr label, and the verse supplies the very path-guidance that its distant fire performs.
The commentary joins fire with guidance on a path; Wisdom's retelling says Wisdom guided the holy people and became a starry flame at night, interpreting Israel's fire-guidance as Wisdom's work.

Wisdom recasts the wilderness pillar as a flaming guide for an unknown journey and a harmless sun for Israel's wandering. That retelling directly develops the commentary's contrast between a helpful distant fire and a destructive one.

basis: warmth and danger of sages' coals
note: Rabbi Eliezer tells disciples to warm themselves by sages' fire yet beware their coals lest they be burned. It preserves the commentary's exact contrast between approaching fire for warmth and suffering it on entering too far.
